title: Level 2 – International Qualified Nurse
subtitle: Mental Health Care
intro: Compassionate Mental Health Care Program Outline Welcome to GNPS Level 2 - International Qualified Nurse. International mental health practice expects nurses to combine therapeutic engagement with structured assessment, evidence-based intervention, legal awareness, cultural safety and multidisciplinary collaboration. This level bridges national nursing preparation with international expectations. It strengthens your ability to assess complex presentations, manage crisis, apply local mental health law, monitor psychotropic treatment and support people across inpatient, community and general healthcare settings. Throughout this level you will strengthen your ability to: Apply internationally recognised recovery and trauma-informed principles Conduct comprehensive mental state and risk assessments Formulate and communicate priority nursing concerns Manage suicide, self-harm, aggression and acute behavioural disturbance Recognise medication toxicity and serious adverse reactions Support people with co-occurring physical health and substance-use needs Apply legal, ethical and least restrictive practice requirements Provide culturally safe care with interpreters and family involvement Coordinate multidisciplinary care, discharge and relapse prevention International practice requires nurses to explain their clinical reasoning, document risk clearly and balance autonomy with safety. Mental health law, admission processes and professional responsibilities may differ between countries, making safe orientation essential. By completing Level 2, you should be able to deliver safe, culturally responsive and evidence-informed mental health nursing while meeting the professional and legal expectations of international healthcare environments.

sections.title: Comprehensive Assessment, Formulation and Care Planning

content.text: International mental health practice expects nurses to integrate mental state findings, history, physical health, trauma, substance use, culture and current risk. Assessment informs a shared formulation and individualised plan rather than a diagnosis alone.
Learning outcomes
Conduct a comprehensive mental health assessment Develop a person-centred nursing formulation
Prioritise mental and physical health needs Communicate findings clearly
Comprehensive Assessment Assessment includes presenting concerns, history, mental state, physical health, medicines, substance use, trauma, social circumstances, strengths and supports.
Risk Formulation Risk formulation considers current thoughts and behaviour, history, dynamic triggers, protective factors and foreseeable changes. A numerical score should not replace judgement.
Care Planning Plans should identify goals, interventions, responsibilities, review timeframes and the person's preferences. Crisis and relapse-prevention plans should be practical and accessible.
Clinical Communication Handover should communicate current mental state, risk, triggers, effective strategies, legal status, medication concerns and required follow-up.

A woman with bipolar disorder presents with reduced sleep, rapid speech, impulsive spending and escalating conflict. The nurse assesses physical health, substance use, risk, supports and previous relapse signs, then develops a shared plan with the multidisciplinary team.
Key learning points
Formulate risk rather than relying on a score Include strengths and protective factors
Integrate physical and mental healthcare Make the plan understandable and actionable

sections.title: Managing Suicide, Self-Harm and Acute Behavioural Disturbance

content.text: High-risk mental health presentations require calm, structured and legally informed care. Nurses should respond to the immediate risk while preserving dignity, therapeutic engagement and future recovery.
Learning outcomes
Assess suicide and self-harm risk comprehensively Respond to aggression and acute disturbance
Apply observation and environmental safety measures Use least restrictive interventions

Suicide Assessment Assessment includes ideation, plan, intent, access to means, past attempts, recent losses, intoxication, command hallucinations and protective factors. Safety planning should be collaborative whenever possible.
Self-Harm Self-harm may serve different functions, including relief from overwhelming emotion. Care should address physical injury, immediate risk and underlying need without punitive responses.
Aggression and Violence Risk Escalating speech, pacing, threats, intoxication and access to weapons require early intervention. Team communication and clear roles are essential.
Observation and Restriction Observation should be purposeful and reviewed. Restrictive interventions require legal authority, documentation, monitoring and post-event review.

A patient states he has hidden tablets at home and plans to take them after discharge. The nurse does not leave him alone, initiates urgent review, collaborates on immediate safety, involves supports with consent where possible and documents the plan and actions clearly.
Key learning points
Take stated plans and access to means seriously Maintain engagement while securing safety
Review restrictive measures frequently Debrief and learn after crisis events

sections.title: Psychopharmacology, Physical Health and Co-occurring Conditions

content.text: People using mental health services may experience medication effects, physical illness and substance-related problems that influence mental state and risk. International nurses are expected to monitor the whole person.
Learning outcomes
Monitor common psychotropic medicines safely Recognise serious adverse reactions and toxicity
Assess physical health needs Support people with co-occurring substance use

Antidepressants and Mood Stabilisers Antidepressants require monitoring for activation, worsening suicidality and serotonin toxicity. Lithium requires blood levels, renal and thyroid monitoring, stable fluid and salt intake, and awareness of toxicity signs.
Antipsychotics Monitoring includes movement disorders, metabolic effects, sedation and cardiac risk. Fever, rigidity and altered consciousness may indicate neuroleptic malignant syndrome.

Physical Health People with severe mental illness experience significant physical-health inequality. Weight, blood pressure, glucose, lipids, smoking, nutrition and preventive care should be addressed.
Substance Use Alcohol, opioids, stimulants and other substances can cause intoxication, withdrawal and co-occurring mental illness. Severe withdrawal and overdose require urgent medical care.

A man taking lithium develops vomiting, coarse tremor and confusion after dehydration. The nurse withholds further doses according to policy, arranges urgent medical review and blood testing, and identifies possible lithium toxicity.
Key learning points
Know the red flags of psychotropic toxicity Do not attribute all physical symptoms to mental illness
Monitor metabolic and cardiovascular health Treat severe withdrawal as a medical emergency

sections.title: Legal, Ethical and Culturally Safe International Practice

content.text: Mental health law and policy differ across jurisdictions, but core principles include dignity, autonomy, confidentiality, proportionality and least restrictive care. International nurses must learn the local legal framework before independent practice.
Learning outcomes
Apply local mental health law and professional standards Balance autonomy, confidentiality and safety
Provide culturally safe and trauma-informed care Collaborate with families and multidisciplinary teams
Consent and Legal Status Nurses should understand voluntary and involuntary care, capacity, consent, review rights and documentation requirements within the local jurisdiction.
Confidentiality and Its Limits Information is protected but may be shared when lawfully required to prevent serious harm. The person should be informed about limits whenever possible.
Cultural Safety Culture influences explanations of distress, help-seeking and family roles. Nurses should ask respectfully and use professional interpreters for complex communication.

Family and Team Collaboration Families may provide important information and support, but involvement should respect consent, confidentiality and safety. Clear multidisciplinary roles improve continuity.

An international nurse is unsure whether a patient can leave an inpatient unit. Rather than relying on previous-country practice, the nurse checks the person's legal status, local policy and senior advice before taking action.
Key learning points
Learn the law and policy of the jurisdiction Use the least restrictive lawful option
Explain confidentiality and its limits Ask rather than assume cultural preferences

End-of-Program Summary By completing GNPS Program 8 - Level 2, you have strengthened your ability to complete comprehensive assessments, formulate risk, manage crisis, monitor psychotropic treatment and practise within international legal and cultural expectations. You are now prepared for Level 3, where the focus moves to leadership, service improvement and global mental health.
